```{r setup}
# Load packages
library(tidyverse)
library(targets)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
library(DiagrammeR)
library(ggpubr)
library(here)
library(scales)


# Source plotting functions needed for the report
# Note: In a strict targets workflow, we usually avoid sourcing files in reports,
# but we need 'replace_funnel_hname' available in the environment.
tar_source(here("R/mod_functions.R"))

# Load Main Data
# Quarto renders with the working directory set to this file's location (R/),
# so point explicitly at the project-root targets store.

dat <- tar_read(analysis_data, store = here::here("_targets"))
hoscode <- tar_read(hoscode_data, store = here::here("_targets"))

# Define Logic Variables
latest_report_year <- max(dat$report_year, na.rm = TRUE)
prev_year <- latest_report_year - 1
start_3yr <- latest_report_year - 2

# Helper Function to load targets dynamically
# This prevents hardcoding "2025" or "au" in chunk code.
# Assumes target naming convention: {base}_{outcome}_{year}_{country}
get_plot_target <- function(base_name, outcome, year, country) {
  target_name <- paste(base_name, outcome, year, country, sep = "_")
  # tar_read_raw() accepts a string name; tar_read() uses NSE and would
  # look for a target literally named `target_name`.
  tar_read_raw(target_name, store = here::here("_targets")) +
    theme(plot.title = element_blank()) +
    labs(
      caption = "Notes: Risk-adjusted mortality rates are adjusted for age, sex, fracture type, ASA grade, pre-fracture mobility and place of residence.",
      width = 110
    ) +
    theme(
      plot.caption = element_text(
        color = "grey10",
        size = 10,
        face = "italic",
        hjust = 0
      ),
      plot.caption.position = "plot"
    )
}

# Pre-calculate counts for text
hosp_counts <- list(
  total = n_distinct(dat$h_name[dat$report_year == latest_report_year]),
  au = n_distinct(dat$h_name[
    dat$report_year == latest_report_year & dat$country == "au"
  ]),
  nz = n_distinct(dat$h_name[
    dat$report_year == latest_report_year & dat$country == "nz"
  ])
)

# Pre-calculate ASA Missingness
calc_asa_miss <- function(data, years) {
  data |>
    filter(report_year %in% years) |>
    group_by(is_missing = is.na(asa_nhfd)) |>
    summarise(n = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(pct = percent(n / sum(n), accuracy = 0.1)) |>
    mutate(txt = paste0(comma(n), " (", pct, ")")) |>
    filter(is_missing)
}

asa_this <- calc_asa_miss(dat, start_3yr:latest_report_year)
asa_last <- calc_asa_miss(dat, (start_3yr - 1):prev_year)
```

## INTRODUCTION

This mortality report includes all hip fracture patients undergoing surgical intervention and having been linked with administrative death data. In New Zealand, all patients are deterministically linked with the National Mortality Collection within the New Zealand Ministry of Health (MOH). In Australia, patients are probabilistically linked with the National Death Index (NDI). There are `r tbl_au_flag$txt[tbl_au_flag$quality_flag == "I"]` cases that are not able to be linked with the NDI due to insufficient information. The unlinked cases are excluded from the analysis in this report.

Mortality has been risk-adjusted for age, sex, pre-morbid level of function (mobility), fracture type, place of residence and ASA grade. Data are presented for two follow-up periods and in two ways. The follow-up periods are 30- and 365-days following presentation with a hip fracture. Both 30-day and 365-day mortality are common benchmarks for hip fracture care. Mortality at 365 days is more likely to be influenced by factors beyond hospital care, but remains an important outcome for patients. 

Age is categorised into 5-year age groups, with the exception of the oldest age group which is 100 years and older. Pre-morbid level of function (mobility) is aggregated into three categories: (i) walk without aids; (ii) walk with 1 aid 2 aids or frame; and (iii) wheelchair bed bound. Fracture type is aggregated into two categories: (i) intracapsular; and (ii) extracapsular. Usual place of residence is aggregated into two categories (i) private residence or (ii) residential care facility or other. ASA grade is aggregated as (i) ASA grades 1 to 2; (ii) ASA grade 3; and (iii) ASA grades 4 and 5, consistent with approaches described in the literature[^1]. 

It is important to note that ASA grade was missing or recorded as unknown in `r asa_this$txt` of patient records in `r start_3yr`-`r latest_report_year` and `r asa_last$txt` of patient records in `r (start_3yr - 1)`-`r prev_year`. There were a very small number of missing and unknown values in covariates other than ASA affecting the statistical model. The missing/unknown values of covariates were handled by multiple imputation by chained equation (MICE)[^2] before constructing the statistical model. The covariates for case-mix adjustment and 30-day mortality status were used in the multiple imputation. Predictive mean matching (PMM)[^3] was used to create 10 imputed datasets and each with 10 iterations in the imputation process. The imputed datasets were then used to construct the statistical model and the results were pooled across the 10 imputed datasets.

In this report, the risk-adjusted mortality rate at 30 days for all surgical patients is presented by year for Australian states for the period 2016-`r latest_report_year`, and New Zealand for the period 2017-`r latest_report_year` (@fig-mort30d-trend), and the risk-adjusted mortality rate at 365 days for all surgical patients is presented by year for Australian states for the period 2016-`r prev_year`, and New Zealand for the period 2017-`r prev_year` (@fig-mort365d-trend). It should be noted that the number of hospitals reporting in each state has grown over time from 2016, which has improved the generalisability of the results in recent years. Mortality rates for South Australia do not include all the hospitals for the period 2018-2020 because patient identifiers were not permitted to be collected for some hospitals, which meant the records were unable to be linked to the National Death Index (NDI). Mortality rate for Tasmania is not reported for 2016 due to a very small number of records. Australia Capital Territory and Northern Territory are included in national rate calculation but not reported individually in this report because there is only one contributing hospital in each state.

Risk-adjusted mortality rates at hospital level are also reported. Results were aggregated over a three-year period to limit the effect of annual fluctuations at hospital level. Pooled data were used for records from each site, from the start of `r start_3yr` to the end of `r latest_report_year` for 30-day mortality and from the start of `r prev_year - 2` to the end of `r prev_year` for 365-day mortality. To ensure a minimum cohort size for stable risk-adjusted mortality estimates, hospitals that did not contribute patient level data for the full three-year period, or had less than 50 surgical patients over the specified three-year period, were not included.  

Data are presented in funnel plots[^4] (@fig-mort30d-nz-funnel, @fig-mort365d-nz-funnel, @fig-mort30d-au-funnel and @fig-mort365d-au-funnel), where each dot represents a hospital site, and the x-axis represents hospital surgical volume. Because of the higher precision from a greater number of patients, data points should ‘funnel’ to a narrower distribution on the right side of the funnel plot. The horizontal line represents the national mortality rate over the three-year time period. Hospitals above the line have a higher risk-adjusted mortality rate than the national rate and those below the line have a lower risk-adjusted mortality rate than the national rate. Control limits set at 2 and 3 standard deviations (95% and 99.7%) are included so that outliers can be identified. 

@fig-mort30d-nz-ctpl, @fig-mort365d-nz-ctpl, @fig-mort30d-au-ctpl and @fig-mort365d-au-ctpl are ‘caterpillar’ plots where each hospital is ranked according to the risk-adjusted mortality rate standardised to the national rate and the ‘legs’ of the caterpillar represent the 95% confidence interval.

For further details on the statistical methodology, please refer to the ANZHFR mortality report github repository (https://github.com/ANZHFR/anzhfr-mortality-report).

## Missingness of covariates used in the multiple imputation

```{r}
#| label: tbl-missing
#| fig-cap: ""
tbl_missing <- dat |>
  select(
    report_year,
    age_cat5,
    sex_2l,
    asa_nhfd,
    walk_nhfd,
    ftype_nhfd,
    uresidence_nhfd,
    mort30d
  ) |>
  arrange(report_year) |>
  mutate(report_year = factor(report_year)) |>
  group_by(report_year) |>
  naniar::miss_var_summary() |>
  mutate(pct_miss = as.numeric(pct_miss) / 100) |>
  mutate(
    txt_miss = paste0(
      n_miss,
      " (",
      scales::percent(pct_miss, accuracy = 0.1),
      ")"
    )
  ) |>
  select(-n_miss, -pct_miss) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = report_year, values_from = txt_miss) |>
  mutate(
    variable = factor(
      variable,
      levels = c(
        "age_cat5",
        "sex_2l",
        "asa_nhfd",
        "walk_nhfd",
        "ftype_nhfd",
        "uresidence_nhfd",
        "mort30d"
      ),
      labels = c(
        "Age",
        "Sex",
        "ASA grade",
        "Pre-fracture mobility",
        "Fracture type",
        "Usual place of residence",
        "30-day mortality"
      )
    )
  ) |>
  arrange(variable)


knitr::kable(tbl_missing)
```
